## Findings (with sources) on RAG evaluation metrics and what they measure

### A) Retrieval-layer metrics (classic IR)
These are used to evaluate *the retriever/ranker* (did we fetch the right chunks/docs, and how well-ranked are they?).

| Metric | What it measures | How computed (high level) | What it misses / failure modes | When to use | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HitRate@k | Whether *at least one* relevant item appears in the top‑k retrieved results | For each query: score = 1 if any relevant chunk is in top‑k else 0; average over queries | Ignores ranking within top‑k and ignores how many relevant items were retrieved (only “at least one”) | Quick sanity check for “does retrieval ever find the right stuff?” | https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/ |
| Recall@k | Coverage: how often relevant documents appear within the top‑k; emphasizes avoiding false negatives | Fraction of relevant items retrieved in top‑k (conceptually: relevant_in_topk / total_relevant) | Can reward retrieving lots of irrelevant items if it also captures relevant ones; depends on having relevance labels / “all relevant items” defined | When missing key evidence is costly; tune top‑k / recall-heavy retrieval | https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/ |
| Precision@k | Purity: how many retrieved top‑k items are actually relevant; emphasizes avoiding false positives | relevant_in_topk / k | Can be high even if you miss important relevant chunks (low recall); depends on relevance labels | When context budget is tight and irrelevant chunks harm generation | https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/ |
| F1@k | Balance between precision@k and recall@k | Harmonic mean of precision@k and recall@k | Hides the tradeoff (two systems with different precision/recall can share same F1); still label-dependent | When you need a single retrieval score but care about both purity and coverage | https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/ |

**What I did *not* find/verify (gap):** In this tool run, I did *not* obtain primary sources for MRR or nDCG definitions/computation, even though they are common retrieval metrics. The Towards Data Science page we captured covers HitRate/Precision/Recall/F1 but not (in the excerpt retrieved) MRR/nDCG. (No verified source in-hand.)

---

### B) Context / grounding-layer metrics (RAGAS)
These measure whether retrieved context is relevant/complete *and* whether the model’s response is supported by it.

| Metric (RAGAS) | What it measures | How computed (high level) | What it misses / failure modes | When to use | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Context Precision | Whether retrieved contexts are ranked with relevant chunks earlier (ranking quality of retrieved_contexts) | “Mean of precision@k for each chunk in the context” using a relevance indicator per rank position (RAGAS describes it as precision@k aggregated over ranks) | Depends on a relevance signal (RAGAS can compare against a reference answer, or without reference by comparing contexts to the response); sensitive to judge/model errors in deciding chunk relevance | When you want to penalize irrelevant chunks early in the context window | https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_precision/ |
| Context Recall | Whether retrieval included the information needed to support the reference answer (coverage of necessary info) | Requires a reference; RAGAS breaks reference into claims and checks if each claim is attributable to retrieved_contexts; recall = fraction of reference claims supported by retrieved context | Requires reference answer; can be brittle if claim extraction/attribution fails; does not directly judge final answer quality | When you have ground-truth answers and want to see if retrieval is the bottleneck | https://docs.ragas.io/en/latest/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_recall/ |
| Faithfulness | Grounding/consistency: whether response claims are supported by retrieved context (hallucination rate proxy) | Identify claims/statements in response; verify each claim can be inferred from retrieved_contexts; score is fraction supported (0–1) | A response can be “faithful” but incomplete or irrelevant; depends on correctness of claim splitting and entailment judgment | When you care about hallucinations and grounding to provided evidence | https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/faithfulness/ |
| Answer (Response) Relevancy | Whether the response addresses the user input (intent match), *not factual accuracy* | Generate synthetic questions from the response; embed original user_input and generated questions; compute mean cosine similarity (average similarity is the score) | Can score high for fluent but wrong answers; sensitive to the question-generation step and embedding model; cosine similarity range not strictly bounded to [0,1] | When you want a reference-free relevance/coverage signal about the generator output | https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/answer_relevance/ |
| Noise Sensitivity | How often the system makes incorrect claims when using relevant/irrelevant retrieved docs (robustness to retrieval noise) | For each response claim: check correctness vs ground truth and whether attributable to relevant/irrelevant retrieved contexts; score in [0,1] where **lower is better** | Requires reference/ground truth; depends on classification of “relevant vs irrelevant” context and claim correctness; may conflate retrieval noise with generator behavior | When you want to quantify how harmful irrelevant retrieval is (and test robustness) | https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/noise_sensitivity/ |
| Context Utilization (listed by RAGAS) | Whether retrieved contexts were “useful” by comparing each context against the generated response (reference-free usefulness signal) | RAGAS page presents it as comparing each retrieved context vs the generated response when no reference is available | I did not fetch a dedicated Context Utilization page; only saw it described inside Context Precision page | When you do not have reference answers but want to see if retrieved text aligns with what the model used/says | Mentioned within https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_precision/ and listed at https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/ |

Additionally, RAGAS lists other metrics available (names only captured here): Context Entities Recall, Multimodal Faithfulness, Multimodal Relevance, plus non-LLM metrics like BLEU/ROUGE/Exact Match etc.  
Source list page: https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/

**What I did *not* find/verify (gap):**
- I did not retrieve primary RAGAS pages for **Context Entities Recall**, **Multimodal Faithfulness**, or **Multimodal Relevance**—only their names from the “available metrics” list. (https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/)
- I did not retrieve a standalone RAGAS page defining **Context Utilization**—only the description embedded in the Context Precision page.

---

### C) Generation-layer / LLM-judge metrics (DeepEval “RAG triad”)
DeepEval documents a “RAG triad” evaluation bundle.

| Metric / framework | What it measures | How computed (high level) | What it misses / failure modes | When to use | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RAG Triad (DeepEval framework) | A referenceless evaluation framework composed of: answer relevancy, faithfulness, contextual relevancy; intended to diagnose prompt vs LLM vs retriever hyperparameters | Not a single formula; it is a set of 3 metrics applied to a test case with `input`, `actual_output`, `retrieval_context` | Being referenceless, it may not detect subtle factual errors if they are consistent with retrieved context or if the judge is weak; depends on LLM-as-judge stability | When you lack labeled ground truth answers and still need structured RAG evaluation | https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval/blob/main/docs/content/guides/guides-rag-triad.mdx |
| Answer Relevancy (DeepEval) | Relevance of the generated answer to the input; LLM-as-judge | DeepEval states it uses an LLM to extract statements from actual_output and classify whether each statement is relevant to input; outputs a score and reason | Does not ensure factual correctness; depends heavily on judge prompts/model | When evaluating generator alignment to question/intent without ground truth | https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval/blob/main/docs/content/docs/(rag)/metrics-answer-relevancy.mdx |
| Faithfulness ≈ groundedness (DeepEval terminology note) | Hallucination/grounding: whether generated answer is supported by retrieval_context | DeepEval guide states faithfulness measures hallucinations; also explicitly: “faithfulness” and “groundedness” are “100% the same thing but just named differently.” | Can be faithful-but-wrong if the retrieved context itself is wrong; may not capture omission/incompleteness | When you want a grounding signal tied to retrieved context | https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval/blob/main/docs/content/guides/guides-rag-triad.mdx |
| Contextual Relevancy (DeepEval) | Whether retrieved chunks are relevant to producing the ideal answer; targets retrieval hyperparameters | DeepEval guide ties it to chunk size/top‑k/embedding model, measuring whether retrieved text chunks are relevant | A relevance-only measure may not guarantee coverage (recall) or support of final claims | When tuning retriever settings with reference-free judging | https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval/blob/main/docs/content/guides/guides-rag-triad.mdx |

**What I did *not* find/verify (gap):**
- I did not fetch DeepEval’s dedicated pages for **FaithfulnessMetric** or **ContextualRelevancyMetric** calculations—only the guide summary and the Answer Relevancy page. So the exact scoring formulas for those two metrics are not verified in-hand.

---

### D) End-to-end / task metrics (as listed by RAGAS)
RAGAS’s “available metrics” list includes standard task/overlap metrics often used for end-to-end evaluation with ground truth (e.g., Exact Match, BLEU, ROUGE, etc.), but the list page does not define them in detail.

| Metric family | What it measures | Evidence captured | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exact Match, BLEU, ROUGE, CHRF, Semantic Similarity, Factual Correctness, String Presence (listed under “Natural Language Comparison”) | Typical end-to-end answer matching / overlap / similarity metrics | Only the fact that these are “available metrics” in RAGAS is captured; definitions not captured in this run | https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/ |

**What I did *not* find/verify (gap):**
- No primary sources captured here explaining how RAGAS computes **Factual Correctness**, **Semantic Similarity**, **ROUGE/BLEU/CHRF**, or how to use them specifically for open-domain QA end-to-end evaluation (EM/F1). Only their availability list is sourced.

---

## Glossary / synonym mapping (sourced where possible)

- **Faithfulness ↔ Groundedness**: DeepEval explicitly states they are “100% the same thing but just named differently.”  
  Source: https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval/blob/main/docs/content/guides/guides-rag-triad.mdx

- **RAGAS “Response Relevancy” / “Answer Relevancy”**: RAGAS page labels “Response Relevancy” and “Answer Relevancy” together and defines it as relevance of response to user input (not factual accuracy).  
  Source: https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/answer_relevance/

- **Context Precision vs Context Recall (RAGAS)**:
  - Context Precision: ranking relevant chunks higher in retrieved_contexts.  
    Source: https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_precision/
  - Context Recall: not missing important information; requires a reference and checks if reference claims are attributable to retrieved_contexts.  
    Source: https://docs.ragas.io/en/latest/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_recall/

---

But before that, it is important to be able to tell if the retrieval mechanism works well and can successfully identify relevant results. After all, retrieving the chunks that contain the answer to the user’s query is the very first step for being able to generate a meaningful answer.
Therefore, this is exactly what we are going to explore in today’s post. In particular, we are going to take a look at some of the most popular metrics for evaluating retrieval and reranking performance.

Why care about measuring retrieval performance
So, our goal is to evaluate how well our embedding model and vector database bring back candidate text chunks. Essentially, what we are trying to find out here is “Are the right documents somewhere in the top-k retrieved set?”, or does our vector search return complete garbage? 🙃 There are several different measures we can utilize to answer this question. Most of them originate from the Information Retrieval field.
Before we begin, it’s useful to distinguish between two types of measures — these are binary and graded relevance measures. More specifically, binary measures characterize a retrieved text chunk either as relevant or irrelevant for answering the user’s query — there is no in between. On the contrary, graded measures assign a relevance value to each text chunk that is retrieved, somewhere in a spectrum ranging from complete irrelevance to complete relevance.
In general, binary measures characterize each chunk as relevant or irrelevant, a hit or a miss, a positive or a negative. As a result, when considering binary retrieval measures, we can end up in one of the following situations:
- True Positive ➔ A result is retrieved in the top k and is indeed relevant to the user’s query; it is correctly retrieved.
- False Positive ➔ A result is retrieved in the top k, but is in fact irrelevant; it is wrongly retrieved.
- True Negative ➔ A result is not retrieved in the top k and is indeed not relevant to the user’s query; it is correctly not retrieved.
- False Negative ➔ A result is not retrieved in the top k, but it was in fact relevant; it is wrongly not retrieved.
As you can imagine, True situations — True Positive and True Negative — are what we are looking for. On the flip side, False situations — False Negative and False Positive — are what we are trying to minimize, but this is a rather conflicting goal. More specifically, in order to include all relevant results that exist (that is, minimize the False Negatives), we need to make our search more inclusive, but by making the search more inclusive, we also risk increasing the False Positives.
Another distinction we can make is between order-unaware and order-aware relevance measures. As their names indicate, order-unaware measures only express whether a relevant result exists in the top k retrieved text chunks, or not. On the flip side, order-aware measures also take into account the ranking in which a text chunk appears, apart from whether it just makes an appearance on the top k chunks.
All retrieval evaluation measures can be calculated for different values of k, thus, we denote them as ‘some measure’@k, like HitRate@k or Precision@k (duh!). Anyways, in the rest of this post, I’ll be exploring some basic binary, order-unaware, retrieval evaluation metrics.
. . .
Some order-unaware, binary measures
Binary order-unaware measures for evaluating retrieval are the most straightforward and intuitive to understand. Thus, they are a great starting point for getting our heads around what exactly we are trying to measure and evaluate. Some common and useful binary, order-unaware measures are HitRate@k, Recall@k, Precision@k, and F1@k. But let’s see all these in some more detail.
🎯 HitRate@K
HitRate@K is the simplest of all measures for evaluating the retrieval evaluation. It is a binary measure indicating whether there is at least one relevant result in the top k retrieved chunks, or not. Thus, it can only take two values: either 1 (if at least one relevant doc exists in the retrieved set), or 0 (if none of the retrieved documents is in reality relevant). Thus, it can range from 0 to 1, with 0 indicating that we only retrieved irrelevant results, and 1 indicating that we only retrieved relevant results (no False Negatives). Recall focuses on the quantity of the retrieved results — how many out of all the relevant results did we manage to find? Thus, it functions well as a retrieval measure for scenarios where we need to find as many relevant results as possible, even by retrieving some irrelevant ones along with them.
Thus, the higher a Recall@k we achieve, the more relevant documents we have retrieved with the vector search, out of all the relevant documents that truly exist. On the contrary, retrieving documents with a bad Recall@k score is a rather bad start for the retrieval step of our RAG pipeline — if the appropriate relevant documents and relevant information aren’t there in the first place, no magical reranking or LLM model is going to fix the situation.

| title | Using the RAG Triad for RAG evaluation | |
|---|---|---|
| sidebar_label | RAG Triad | |
| languages | 
 | 
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a powerful way for LLMs to generate responses based on context beyond the scope of its training data by supplying it with external data as additional context. These supporting context comes in the form of text chunks, which are usually parsed, vectorized, and indexed in vector databases for fast retrieval at inference time, hence the name retrieval, augmented, generation.
In a previous guide, we explored how the generator in a RAG pipeline can hallucinate despite being supplied additional context, while the retriever can often fail to retrieve the correct and relevant context to generate the optimal answer. This is why evaluating RAG pipelines are important and where the RAG triad comes into play.
The RAG triad is composed of three RAG evaluation metrics: answer relevancy, faithfulness, and contextual relevancy. If a RAG pipeline scores high on all three metrics, we can confidently say that our RAG pipeline is using the optimal hyperparameters. This is because each metric in the RAG triad corresponds to a certain hyperparameter in the RAG pipeline. For instance:
- 
Answer relevancy: the answer relevancy metric determines how relevant the answers generated by your RAG generator is. Since LLMs nowadays are getting pretty good at reasoning, it is mainly the prompt template hyperparameter instead of the LLM you are iterating on when working with the answer relevancy metric. To be more specific, a low answer relevancy score signifies that you need to improve examples used in prompt templates for better in-context learning, or include more fine-grained prompting for better instruction following capabilities to generate more relevant responses. 
- 
Faithfulness: the faithfulness metric determines how much the answers generated by your RAG generator are hallucinations. This concerns the LLM hyperparameter, and you'll want to switch to a different LLM or even fine-tune your own if your LLM is unable to leverage the retrieval context supplied to it to generate grounded answers. :::info You might also see the faithfulness metric called groundedness instead in other places. They are 100% the same thing but just named differently. ::: 
- 
Contextual Relevancy: the contextual relevancy metric determines whether the text chunks retrieved by your RAG retriever are relevant to producing the ideal answer for a user input. This concerns the chunk size, top-K and embedding model hyperparameter. A good embedding model ensures you're able to retrieve text chunks that are semantically similar to the embedded user query, while a good combination of chunk size and top-K ensures you only select the most important bits of information in your knowledge base. 
:::caution You might have noticed we didn't mention the contextual precision and contextual recall metric. For those wondering, this is because contextual precision and recall requires a labelled expected answer (i.e. the ideal answer to a user input) which may not be possible for everyone, which is why this guide serves as full referenceless RAG evaluation guide. :::
Using the RAG triad of metrics in deepeval is as simple as writing a few lines of code. First, create a test case to represent a user query, retrieved text chunks, and an LLM response:
from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase
test_case = LLMTestCase(input="...", actual_output="...", retrieval_context=["..."])Here, input is the user query, actual_output is the LLM generated response, and retrieval_context is a list of strings representing the retrieved text chunks. Then, define the RAG triad metrics:
from deepeval.metrics import AnswerRelevancyMetric, FaithfulnessMetric, ContextualRelevancyMetric
...
answer_relevancy = AnswerRelevancyMetric()
faithfulness = FaithfulnessMetric()
contextual_relevancy = ContextualRelevancyMetric():::tip You can find how these metrics are implemented and calculated on their respective documentation pages:
:::
Lastly, evaluate your test case using these metrics:
from deepeval import evaluate
...
evaluate(test_cases=[test_case], metrics=[answer_relevancy, faithfulness, contextual_relevancy])Congratulations 🎉! You've learnt everything you need to know for the RAG triad.
As you scale up your RAG evaluation efforts, you can simply supply more test cases to the list of test_cases in the evaluate() function and more importantly, you can also generate synthetic datasets using deepeval to test your RAG application at scale.

Context Precision
Context Precision is a metric that evaluates the retriever's ability to rank relevant chunks higher than irrelevant ones for a given query in the retrieved context. Specifically, it assesses the degree to which relevant chunks in the retrieved context are placed at the top of the ranking.
It is calculated as the mean of the precision@k for each chunk in the context. Precision@k is the ratio of the number of relevant chunks at rank k to the total number of chunks at rank k.
Where \(K\) is the total number of chunks in retrieved_contexts and \(v_k \in \{0, 1\}\) is the relevance indicator at rank \(k\).
Examples
Context Precision
The ContextPrecision metric evaluates whether retrieved contexts are useful for answering a question by comparing each context against a reference answer. Use this when you have a reference answer available.
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from ragas.llms import llm_factory
from ragas.metrics.collections import ContextPrecision
# Setup LLM
client = AsyncOpenAI()
llm = llm_factory("gpt-4o-mini", client=client)
# Create metric
scorer = ContextPrecision(llm=llm)
# Evaluate
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    reference="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=[
        "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
        "The Brandenburg Gate is located in Berlin."
    ]
)
print(f"Context Precision Score: {result.value}")

Response Relevancy
Answer Relevancy
The Answer Relevancy metric measures how relevant a response is to the user input. It ranges from 0 to 1, with higher scores indicating better alignment with the user input.
An answer is considered relevant if it directly and appropriately addresses the original question. This metric focuses on how well the answer matches the intent of the question, without evaluating factual accuracy. It penalizes answers that are incomplete or include unnecessary details.
This metric is calculated using the user_input and the response as follows:  
- Generate a set of artificial questions (default is 3) based on the response. These questions are designed to reflect the content of the response.
- Compute the cosine similarity between the embedding of the user input (\(E_o\)) and the embedding of each generated question (\(E_{g_i}\)).
- Take the average of these cosine similarity scores to get the Answer Relevancy:
Where:
- \(E_{g_i}\): Embedding of the \(i^{th}\) generated question.
- \(E_o\): Embedding of the user input.
- \(N\): Number of generated questions (default is 3, configurable via strictness parameter).  
Note: While the score usually falls between 0 and 1, it is not guaranteed due to cosine similarity's mathematical range of -1 to 1.
Example
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from ragas.llms import llm_factory
from ragas.embeddings.base import embedding_factory
from ragas.metrics.collections import AnswerRelevancy
# Setup LLM and embeddings
client = AsyncOpenAI()
llm = llm_factory("gpt-4o-mini", client=client)
embeddings = embedding_factory("openai", model="text-embedding-3-small", client=client)
# Create metric
scorer = AnswerRelevancy(llm=llm, embeddings=embeddings)
# Evaluate
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="When was the first super bowl?",
    response="The first superbowl was held on Jan 15, 1967"
)
print(f"Answer Relevancy Score: {result.value}")

Synchronous Usage
If you prefer synchronous code, you can use the .score() method instead of .ascore():
How It’s Calculated
Example
Question: Where is France and what is it's capital?
Low relevance answer: France is in western Europe.
High relevance answer: France is in western Europe and Paris is its capital.
To calculate the relevance of the answer to the given question, we follow two steps:
- 
Step 1: Reverse-engineer 'n' variants of the question from the generated answer using a Large Language Model (LLM). For instance, for the first answer, the LLM might generate the following possible questions: - Question 1: "In which part of Europe is France located?"
- Question 2: "What is the geographical location of France within Europe?"
- Question 3: "Can you identify the region of Europe where France is situated?"
 
- 
Step 2: Calculate the mean cosine similarity between the generated questions and the actual question. 
The underlying concept is that if the answer correctly addresses the question, it is highly probable that the original question can be reconstructed solely from the answer.

But before that, it is important to be able to tell if the retrieval mechanism works well and can successfully identify relevant results. After all, retrieving the chunks that contain the answer to the user’s query is the very first step for being able to generate a meaningful answer.
Therefore, this is exactly what we are going to explore in today’s post. In particular, we are going to take a look at some of the most popular metrics for evaluating retrieval and reranking performance.

Why care about measuring retrieval performance
So, our goal is to evaluate how well our embedding model and vector database bring back candidate text chunks. Essentially, what we are trying to find out here is “Are the right documents somewhere in the top-k retrieved set?”, or does our vector search return complete garbage? 🙃 There are several different measures we can utilize to answer this question. Most of them originate from the Information Retrieval field.
Before we begin, it’s useful to distinguish between two types of measures — these are binary and graded relevance measures. More specifically, binary measures characterize a retrieved text chunk either as relevant or irrelevant for answering the user’s query — there is no in between. On the contrary, graded measures assign a relevance value to each text chunk that is retrieved, somewhere in a spectrum ranging from complete irrelevance to complete relevance.
In general, binary measures characterize each chunk as relevant or irrelevant, a hit or a miss, a positive or a negative. As a result, when considering binary retrieval measures, we can end up in one of the following situations:
- True Positive ➔ A result is retrieved in the top k and is indeed relevant to the user’s query; it is correctly retrieved.
- False Positive ➔ A result is retrieved in the top k, but is in fact irrelevant; it is wrongly retrieved.
- True Negative ➔ A result is not retrieved in the top k and is indeed not relevant to the user’s query; it is correctly not retrieved.
- False Negative ➔ A result is not retrieved in the top k, but it was in fact relevant; it is wrongly not retrieved.
As you can imagine, True situations — True Positive and True Negative — are what we are looking for. On the flip side, False situations — False Negative and False Positive — are what we are trying to minimize, but this is a rather conflicting goal. More specifically, in order to include all relevant results that exist (that is, minimize the False Negatives), we need to make our search more inclusive, but by making the search more inclusive, we also risk increasing the False Positives.
Another distinction we can make is between order-unaware and order-aware relevance measures. As their names indicate, order-unaware measures only express whether a relevant result exists in the top k retrieved text chunks, or not. On the flip side, order-aware measures also take into account the ranking in which a text chunk appears, apart from whether it just makes an appearance on the top k chunks.
All retrieval evaluation measures can be calculated for different values of k, thus, we denote them as ‘some measure’@k, like HitRate@k or Precision@k (duh!). Anyways, in the rest of this post, I’ll be exploring some basic binary, order-unaware, retrieval evaluation metrics.

Some order-unaware, binary measures
Binary order-unaware measures for evaluating retrieval are the most straightforward and intuitive to understand. Thus, they are a great starting point for getting our heads around what exactly we are trying to measure and evaluate. Some common and useful binary, order-unaware measures are HitRate@k, Recall@k, Precision@k, and F1@k. But let’s see all these in some more detail.
🎯 HitRate@K
HitRate@K is the simplest of all measures for evaluating the retrieval evaluation. It is a binary measure indicating whether there is at least one relevant result in the top k retrieved chunks, or not. Thus, it can only take two values: either 1 (if at least one relevant doc exists in the retrieved set), or 0 (if none of the retrieved documents is in reality relevant). Recall focuses on the quantity of the retrieved results — how many out of all the relevant results did we manage to find? Thus, it functions well as a retrieval measure for scenarios where we need to find as many relevant results as possible, even by retrieving some irrelevant ones along with them.
Thus, the higher a Recall@k we achieve, the more relevant documents we have retrieved with the vector search, out of all the relevant documents that truly exist. On the contrary, retrieving documents with a bad Recall@k score is a rather bad start for the retrieval step of our RAG pipeline — if the appropriate relevant documents and relevant information aren’t there in the first place, no magical reranking or LLM model is going to fix the situation.

That is, retrieving results that we are sure are relevant, even if this means we mistakenly reject some relevant results.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a powerful way for LLMs to generate responses based on context beyond the scope of its training data by supplying it with external data as additional context. These supporting context comes in the form of text chunks, which are usually parsed, vectorized, and indexed in vector databases for fast retrieval at inference time, hence the name retrieval, augmented, generation.
In a previous guide, we explored how the generator in a RAG pipeline can hallucinate despite being supplied additional context, while the retriever can often fail to retrieve the correct and relevant context to generate the optimal answer. This is why evaluating RAG pipelines are important and where the RAG triad comes into play.
The RAG triad is composed of three RAG evaluation metrics: answer relevancy, faithfulness, and contextual relevancy. If a RAG pipeline scores high on all three metrics, we can confidently say that our RAG pipeline is using the optimal hyperparameters. This is because each metric in the RAG triad corresponds to a certain hyperparameter in the RAG pipeline. For instance:
- 
Answer relevancy: the answer relevancy metric determines how relevant the answers generated by your RAG generator is. Since LLMs nowadays are getting pretty good at reasoning, it is mainly the prompt template hyperparameter instead of the LLM you are iterating on when working with the answer relevancy metric. To be more specific, a low answer relevancy score signifies that you need to improve examples used in prompt templates for better in-context learning, or include more fine-grained prompting for better instruction following capabilities to generate more relevant responses. 
- 
Faithfulness: the faithfulness metric determines how much the answers generated by your RAG generator are hallucinations. This concerns the LLM hyperparameter, and you'll want to switch to a different LLM or even fine-tune your own if your LLM is unable to leverage the retrieval context supplied to it to generate grounded answers. :::info You might also see the faithfulness metric called groundedness instead in other places. They are 100% the same thing but just named differently. ::: 
- 
Contextual Relevancy: the contextual relevancy metric determines whether the text chunks retrieved by your RAG retriever are relevant to producing the ideal answer for a user input. This concerns the chunk size, top-K and embedding model hyperparameter. A good embedding model ensures you're able to retrieve text chunks that are semantically similar to the embedded user query, while a good combination of chunk size and top-K ensures you only select the most important bits of information in your knowledge base. 
:::caution You might have noticed we didn't mention the contextual precision and contextual recall metric. For those wondering, this is because contextual precision and recall requires a labelled expected answer (i.e. the ideal answer to a user input) which may not be possible for everyone, which is why this guide serves as full referenceless RAG evaluation guide. :::
Using the RAG triad of metrics in deepeval is as simple as writing a few lines of code. First, create a test case to represent a user query, retrieved text chunks, and an LLM response:
from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase
test_case = LLMTestCase(input="...", actual_output="...", retrieval_context=["..."])Here, input is the user query, actual_output is the LLM generated response, and retrieval_context is a list of strings representing the retrieved text chunks. Then, define the RAG triad metrics:
from deepeval.metrics import AnswerRelevancyMetric, FaithfulnessMetric, ContextualRelevancyMetric
...
answer_relevancy = AnswerRelevancyMetric()
faithfulness = FaithfulnessMetric()
contextual_relevancy = ContextualRelevancyMetric():::tip You can find how these metrics are implemented and calculated on their respective documentation pages:
:::
Lastly, evaluate your test case using these metrics:
from deepeval import evaluate
...
evaluate(test_cases=[test_case], metrics=[answer_relevancy, faithfulness, contextual_relevancy])Congratulations 🎉! You've learnt everything you need to know for the RAG triad.
As you scale up your RAG evaluation efforts, you can simply supply more test cases to the list of test_cases in the evaluate() function and more importantly, you can also generate synthetic datasets using deepeval to test your RAG application at scale.

Context Precision
Context Precision is a metric that evaluates the retriever's ability to rank relevant chunks higher than irrelevant ones for a given query in the retrieved context. Specifically, it assesses the degree to which relevant chunks in the retrieved context are placed at the top of the ranking.
It is calculated as the mean of the precision@k for each chunk in the context. Precision@k is the ratio of the number of relevant chunks at rank k to the total number of chunks at rank k.
Where \(K\) is the total number of chunks in retrieved_contexts and \(v_k \in \{0, 1\}\) is the relevance indicator at rank \(k\).
Examples
Context Precision
The ContextPrecision metric evaluates whether retrieved contexts are useful for answering a question by comparing each context against a reference answer. Use this when you have a reference answer available.
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from ragas.llms import llm_factory
from ragas.metrics.collections import ContextPrecision
# Setup LLM
client = AsyncOpenAI()
llm = llm_factory("gpt-4o-mini", client=client)
# Create metric
scorer = ContextPrecision(llm=llm)
# Evaluate
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    reference="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=[
        "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
        "The Brandenburg Gate is located in Berlin."
    ]
)
print(f"Context Precision Score: {result.value}")

Context Recall
Context Recall measures how many of the relevant documents (or pieces of information) were successfully retrieved. It focuses on not missing important results. Higher recall means fewer relevant documents were left out. In short, recall is about not missing anything important.
Since it is about not missing anything, calculating context recall always requires a reference to compare against. The LLM-based Context Recall metric uses reference as a proxy to reference_contexts, which makes it easier to use as annotating reference contexts can be very time-consuming. To estimate context recall from the reference, the reference is broken down into claims, and each claim is analyzed to determine whether it can be attributed to the retrieved context or not. In an ideal scenario, all claims in the reference answer should be attributable to the retrieved context.

Response Relevancy
Answer Relevancy
The Answer Relevancy metric measures how relevant a response is to the user input. It ranges from 0 to 1, with higher scores indicating better alignment with the user input.
An answer is considered relevant if it directly and appropriately addresses the original question. This metric focuses on how well the answer matches the intent of the question, without evaluating factual accuracy. It penalizes answers that are incomplete or include unnecessary details.
This metric is calculated using the user_input and the response as follows:  
- Generate a set of artificial questions (default is 3) based on the response. These questions are designed to reflect the content of the response.
- Compute the cosine similarity between the embedding of the user input (\(E_o\)) and the embedding of each generated question (\(E_{g_i}\)).
- Take the average of these cosine similarity scores to get the Answer Relevancy:
Where:
- \(E_{g_i}\): Embedding of the \(i^{th}\) generated question.
- \(E_o\): Embedding of the user input.
- \(N\): Number of generated questions (default is 3, configurable via strictness parameter).  
Note: While the score usually falls between 0 and 1, it is not guaranteed due to cosine similarity's mathematical range of -1 to 1.
Example
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from ragas.llms import llm_factory
from ragas.embeddings.base import embedding_factory
from ragas.metrics.collections import AnswerRelevancy
# Setup LLM and embeddings
client = AsyncOpenAI()
llm = llm_factory("gpt-4o-mini", client=client)
embeddings = embedding_factory("openai", model="text-embedding-3-small", client=client)
# Create metric
scorer = AnswerRelevancy(llm=llm, embeddings=embeddings)
# Evaluate
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="When was the first super bowl?",
    response="The first superbowl was held on Jan 15, 1967"
)
print(f"Answer Relevancy Score: {result.value}")

How It’s Calculated
Example
Question: Where is France and what is it's capital?
Low relevance answer: France is in western Europe.
High relevance answer: France is in western Europe and Paris is its capital.
To calculate the relevance of the answer to the given question, we follow two steps:
- 
Step 1: Reverse-engineer 'n' variants of the question from the generated answer using a Large Language Model (LLM). For instance, for the first answer, the LLM might generate the following possible questions: - Question 1: "In which part of Europe is France located?"
- Question 2: "What is the geographical location of France within Europe?"
- Question 3: "Can you identify the region of Europe where France is situated?"
 
- 
Step 2: Calculate the mean cosine similarity between the generated questions and the actual question. 
The underlying concept is that if the answer correctly addresses the question, it is highly probable that the original question can be reconstructed solely from the answer.

- \(RCE\): The set of entities in the retrieved contexts.

## Findings (with sources) on RAG evaluation metrics and what they measure

### A) Retrieval-layer metrics (classic IR)
These are used to evaluate *the retriever/ranker* (did we fetch the right chunks/docs, and how well-ranked are they?).

| Metric | What it measures | How computed (high level) | What it misses / failure modes | When to use | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HitRate@k | Whether *at least one* relevant item appears in the top‑k retrieved results | For each query: score = 1 if any relevant chunk is in top‑k else 0; average over queries | Ignores ranking within top‑k and ignores how many relevant items were retrieved (only “at least one”) | Quick sanity check for “does retrieval ever find the right stuff?” | https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/ |
| Recall@k | Coverage: how often relevant documents appear within the top‑k; emphasizes avoiding false negatives | Fraction of relevant items retrieved in top‑k (conceptually: relevant_in_topk / total_relevant) | Can reward retrieving lots of irrelevant items if it also captures relevant ones; depends on having relevance labels / “all relevant items” defined | When missing key evidence is costly; tune top‑k / recall-heavy retrieval | https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/ |
| Precision@k | Purity: how many retrieved top‑k items are actually relevant; emphasizes avoiding false positives | relevant_in_topk / k | Can be high even if you miss important relevant chunks (low recall); depends on relevance labels | When context budget is tight and irrelevant chunks harm generation | https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/ |
| F1@k | Balance between precision@k and recall@k | Harmonic mean of precision@k and recall@k | Hides the tradeoff (two systems with different precision/recall can share same F1); still label-dependent | When you need a single retrieval score but care about both purity and coverage | https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/ |

**What I did *not* find/verify (gap):** In this tool run, I did *not* obtain primary sources for MRR or nDCG definitions/computation, even though they are common retrieval metrics. The Towards Data Science page we captured covers HitRate/Precision/Recall/F1 but not (in the excerpt retrieved) MRR/nDCG. (No verified source in-hand.)

---

### B) Context / grounding-layer metrics (RAGAS)
These measure whether retrieved context is relevant/complete *and* whether the model’s response is supported by it.

| Metric (RAGAS) | What it measures | How computed (high level) | What it misses / failure modes | When to use | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Context Precision | Whether retrieved contexts are ranked with relevant chunks earlier (ranking quality of retrieved_contexts) | “Mean of precision@k for each chunk in the context” using a relevance indicator per rank position (RAGAS describes it as precision@k aggregated over ranks) | Depends on a relevance signal (RAGAS can compare against a reference answer, or without reference by comparing contexts to the response); sensitive to judge/model errors in deciding chunk relevance | When you want to penalize irrelevant chunks early in the context window | https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_precision/ |
| Context Recall | Whether retrieval included the information needed to support the reference answer (coverage of necessary info) | Requires a reference; RAGAS breaks reference into claims and checks if each claim is attributable to retrieved_contexts; recall = fraction of reference claims supported by retrieved context | Requires reference answer; can be brittle if claim extraction/attribution fails; does not directly judge final answer quality | When you have ground-truth answers and want to see if retrieval is the bottleneck | https://docs.ragas.io/en/latest/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_recall/ |
| Faithfulness | Grounding/consistency: whether response claims are supported by retrieved context (hallucination rate proxy) | Identify claims/statements in response; verify each claim can be inferred from retrieved_contexts; score is fraction supported (0–1) | A response can be “faithful” but incomplete or irrelevant; depends on correctness of claim splitting and entailment judgment | When you care about hallucinations and grounding to provided evidence | https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/faithfulness/ |
| Answer (Response) Relevancy | Whether the response addresses the user input (intent match), *not factual accuracy* | Generate synthetic questions from the response; embed original user_input and generated questions; compute mean cosine similarity (average similarity is the score) | Can score high for fluent but wrong answers; sensitive to the question-generation step and embedding model; cosine similarity range not strictly bounded to [0,1] | When you want a reference-free relevance/coverage signal about the generator output | https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/answer_relevance/ |
| Noise Sensitivity | How often the system makes incorrect claims when using relevant/irrelevant retrieved docs (robustness to retrieval noise) | For each response claim: check correctness vs ground truth and whether attributable to relevant/irrelevant retrieved contexts; score in [0,1] where **lower is better** | Requires reference/ground truth; depends on classification of “relevant vs irrelevant” context and claim correctness; may conflate retrieval noise with generator behavior | When you want to quantify how harmful irrelevant retrieval is (and test robustness) | https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/noise_sensitivity/ |
| Context Utilization (listed by RAGAS) | Whether retrieved contexts were “useful” by comparing each context against the generated response (reference-free usefulness signal) | RAGAS page presents it as comparing each retrieved context vs the generated response when no reference is available | I did not fetch a dedicated Context Utilization page; only saw it described inside Context Precision page | When you do not have reference answers but want to see if retrieved text aligns with what the model used/says | Mentioned within https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_precision/ and listed at https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/ |

Additionally, RAGAS lists other metrics available (names only captured here): Context Entities Recall, Multimodal Faithfulness, Multimodal Relevance, plus non-LLM metrics like BLEU/ROUGE/Exact Match etc.  
Source list page: https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/

**What I did *not* find/verify (gap):**

- I did not retrieve a standalone RAGAS page defining **Context Utilization**—only the description embedded in the Context Precision page.

---

### C) Generation-layer / LLM-judge metrics (DeepEval “RAG triad”)
DeepEval documents a “RAG triad” evaluation bundle.

| Metric / framework | What it measures | How computed (high level) | What it misses / failure modes | When to use | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RAG Triad (DeepEval framework) | A referenceless evaluation framework composed of: answer relevancy, faithfulness, contextual relevancy; intended to diagnose prompt vs LLM vs retriever hyperparameters | Not a single formula; it is a set of 3 metrics applied to a test case with `input`, `actual_output`, `retrieval_context` | Being referenceless, it may not detect subtle factual errors if they are consistent with retrieved context or if the judge is weak; depends on LLM-as-judge stability | When you lack labeled ground truth answers and still need structured RAG evaluation | https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval/blob/main/docs/content/guides/guides-rag-triad.mdx |
| Answer Relevancy (DeepEval) | Relevance of the generated answer to the input; LLM-as-judge | DeepEval states it uses an LLM to extract statements from actual_output and classify whether each statement is relevant to input; outputs a score and reason | Does not ensure factual correctness; depends heavily on judge prompts/model | When evaluating generator alignment to question/intent without ground truth | https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval/blob/main/docs/content/docs/(rag)/metrics-answer-relevancy.mdx |
| Faithfulness ≈ groundedness (DeepEval terminology note) | Hallucination/grounding: whether generated answer is supported by retrieval_context | DeepEval guide states faithfulness measures hallucinations; also explicitly: “faithfulness” and “groundedness” are “100% the same thing but just named differently.” | Can be faithful-but-wrong if the retrieved context itself is wrong; may not capture omission/incompleteness | When you want a grounding signal tied to retrieved context | https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval/blob/main/docs/content/guides/guides-rag-triad.mdx |
| Contextual Relevancy (DeepEval) | Whether retrieved chunks are relevant to producing the ideal answer; targets retrieval hyperparameters | DeepEval guide ties it to chunk size/top‑k/embedding model, measuring whether retrieved text chunks are relevant | A relevance-only measure may not guarantee coverage (recall) or support of final claims | When tuning retriever settings with reference-free judging | https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval/blob/main/docs/content/guides/guides-rag-triad.mdx |

**What I did *not* find/verify (gap):**
- I did not fetch DeepEval’s dedicated pages for **FaithfulnessMetric** or **ContextualRelevancyMetric** calculations—only the guide summary and the Answer Relevancy page. So the exact scoring formulas for those two metrics are not verified in-hand.

---

### D) End-to-end / task metrics (as listed by RAGAS)
RAGAS’s “available metrics” list includes standard task/overlap metrics often used for end-to-end evaluation with ground truth (e.g., Exact Match, BLEU, ROUGE, etc.), but the list page does not define them in detail.

| Metric family | What it measures | Evidence captured | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exact Match, BLEU, ROUGE, CHRF, Semantic Similarity, Factual Correctness, String Presence (listed under “Natural Language Comparison”) | Typical end-to-end answer matching / overlap / similarity metrics | Only the fact that these are “available metrics” in RAGAS is captured; definitions not captured in this run | https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/ |

---

## Glossary / synonym mapping (sourced where possible)

- **Faithfulness ↔ Groundedness**: DeepEval explicitly states they are “100% the same thing but just named differently.”  
  Source: https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval/blob/main/docs/content/guides/guides-rag-triad.mdx

## Findings: retrieval metrics (evaluate the retriever/ranker)

### Hit Rate@k (a.k.a. Hit@k)
- **What it measures:** Whether **at least one** relevant document appears in the top‑k retrieved set (binary success per query).
- **Definition (quoted):** “HitRate@K… is a binary measure indicating whether there is at least one relevant result in the top k retrieved chunks, or not… either 1… or 0…”【https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/】
- **Computation notes:** For each query: `1 if any relevant in top-k else 0`; average across queries.【https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/】

### Recall@k
- **What it measures:** Coverage of relevant items in the top‑k (focus on avoiding false negatives).
- **Definition (quoted):** “Recall@K expresses how often the relevant documents appear within the top k retrieved documents… calculated as follows… can range from 0 to 1…”【https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/】
- **Computation notes:** Typically `(# relevant retrieved in top-k) / (# relevant total)` per query; average across queries.【https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/】
- **Gap:** This source discusses recall intuitively and shows a formula image, but the extracted text does **not** include the explicit denominator phrase; use standard IR definition cautiously (needs a fully text-extracted formal source).

### Precision@k
- **What it measures:** Purity of the top‑k results (focus on avoiding false positives).
- **Definition (quoted):** “Precision@k indicates how many of the top k retrieved documents are indeed relevant… ‘Out of the items that we retrieved, how many are correct?’… range from 0 to 1…”【https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/】
- **Computation notes:** Commonly `(# relevant retrieved in top-k)/k` per query; average across queries.【https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/】
- **Gap:** As above, the exact formula is in an image on that page and not fully captured in extracted text.

### Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)
- **What it measures:** How early the **first** relevant item appears in the ranked list.
- **Definition (quoted):** “Mean reciprocal rank… produces a list… ordered by probability of correctness. The reciprocal rank… is… inverse of the rank of the first correct answer… The mean reciprocal rank is the average of the reciprocal ranks…”【https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_reciprocal_rank】
- **Computation notes:** For each query, `RR = 1/(rank of first relevant)` else `0`; then average across queries Q.【https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_reciprocal_rank】

### nDCG (normalized discounted cumulative gain)
- **What it measures:** Ranking quality with **graded relevance** and position discounting; normalized to compare across queries.
- **Definition (quoted):** DCG “is a measure of ranking quality…”; DCG “sums the usefulness… discounted by their position…”; “NDCG is DCG normalized by the maximum possible DCG…”【https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discounted_cumulative_gain】
- **Computation notes:** Compute DCG with log discount by rank; compute IDCG (ideal DCG) by sorting by relevance; `nDCG = DCG/IDCG` (often at depth k, i.e., nDCG@k).【https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discounted_cumulative_gain】

## Findings: context metrics (evaluate retrieved context quality for answering)

- **What it measures:** Coverage of relevant items in the top‑k (focus on avoiding false negatives).
- **Definition (quoted):** “Recall@K expresses how often the relevant documents appear within the top k retrieved documents… calculated as follows… can range from 0 to 1…”【https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/】
- **Computation notes:** Typically `(# relevant retrieved in top-k) / (# relevant total)` per query; average across queries.【https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-evaluate-retrieval-quality-in-rag-pipelines-precisionk-recallk-and-f1k/】

- **What it measures:** factual alignment of response to reference using claim decomposition + NLI overlap.

### Error rate
- **Definition + formula:** “Error rate is the proportion of requests or operations that fail versus total attempts… Formal: error rate = failed events / total events over a defined window.”【https://sreschool.com/blog/error-rate/】

### Throughput / QPS / tokens-per-second
- **Definition in a major cloud doc (throughput equation):**
  - Google Cloud defines throughput per second in a generative AI setting and gives:

  - It also states: “Provisioned Throughput is measured in tokens per second, characters per second, or images per second… [and] isn’t measured solely based on queries per minute (QPM).”【https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/provisioned-throughput/measure-provisioned-throughput】

- **Definition:** “Cost per request is the calculated monetary cost of processing one logical request through all infrastructure and services, including direct and allocated shared costs.”【https://finopsschool.com/blog/cost-per-request/】

- **Definition (what’s tracked):** Langfuse “tracks the usage and cost of every LLM call…” and records:
  - “Usage details: number of units consumed per usage type”
  - “Cost details: USD cost per usage type”【https://langfuse.com/docs/observability/features/token-and-cost-tracking】
- **How cost can be computed:** Langfuse “multiplies those prices by the observation's usage to calculate cost.”【https://langfuse.com/docs/observability/features/token-and-cost-tracking】

- Elastic explicitly warns that n-gram metrics are limited: “they fall short when it comes to assessing the fluency, coherence, and overall meaning of passages… lack semantic knowledge, making them blind to semantic variations…” and “studies have revealed that the correlation between BLEU and ROUGE scores and human judgments is actually quite low.”【https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/evaluating-rag-metrics】

*Gap:* I did **not** find, in accessible sources this run, a directly stated limitation of **Exact Match / token-F1** specifically regarding factuality/grounding in RAG (only general overlap-metric limitations were sourced from Elastic).

(Previous round used an Inferensys glossary; critique requested recognized frameworks instead.)

# Metrics used to evaluate RAG systems (and what each measures)

RAG (retrieval‑augmented generation) evaluation is usually split into: **retrieval/ranking quality**, **context quality for answering**, **answer quality vs. the question**, **grounding/faithfulness**, and **production/system behavior**.

> Note on sources: some classic IR metrics are best defined in textbooks/TREC guides; in this run, only **MRR** was found with a canonical TREC definition. For **Precision@k/Recall@k/MAP/nDCG** we use a combination of Wikipedia (classic IR definitions) plus explicit @k formulas from EvidentlyAI (clear text formulas, but not a canonical IR textbook).

## 1) Retrieval / ranking metrics (evaluate the retriever or reranker)

These metrics assume you can label which retrieved items are **relevant** (binary or graded). They measure whether the *right* documents/chunks are retrieved and how well they are ranked.

| Metric | What it measures in RAG | How it’s computed (high level) | When it’s appropriate / caveats | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Precision@k (P@k)** | **Purity** of the top‑k retrieved items (how many retrieved chunks are actually relevant). High P@k means less irrelevant context fed to the LLM. | P@k = (# relevant items in top‑k) / k. | Requires relevance labels. Can look good even if you miss key info (low recall). | EvidentlyAI defines P@k and gives the formula.【https://www.evidentlyai.com/ranking-metrics/precision-recall-at-k】 Wikipedia gives the general (non‑@k) precision definition.【https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaluation_measures_(information_retrieval)】 |

# Metrics used to evaluate RAG systems (and what each measures)

RAG (retrieval‑augmented generation) evaluation is usually split into: **retrieval/ranking quality**, **context quality for answering**, **answer quality vs. the question**, **grounding/faithfulness**, and **production/system behavior**.

> Note on sources: some classic IR metrics are best defined in textbooks/TREC guides; in this run, only **MRR** was found with a canonical TREC definition. For **Precision@k/Recall@k/MAP/nDCG** we use a combination of Wikipedia (classic IR definitions) plus explicit @k formulas from EvidentlyAI (clear text formulas, but not a canonical IR textbook).

## 1) Retrieval / ranking metrics (evaluate the retriever or reranker)

These metrics assume you can label which retrieved items are **relevant** (binary or graded). They measure whether the *right* documents/chunks are retrieved and how well they are ranked.

| Metric | What it measures in RAG | How it’s computed (high level) | When it’s appropriate / caveats | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Precision@k (P@k)** | **Purity** of the top‑k retrieved items (how many retrieved chunks are actually relevant). High P@k means less irrelevant context fed to the LLM. | P@k = (# relevant items in top‑k) / k. | Requires relevance labels. Can look good even if you miss key info (low recall). | EvidentlyAI defines P@k and gives the formula.【https://www.evidentlyai.com/ranking-metrics/precision-recall-at-k】 Wikipedia gives the general (non‑@k) precision definition.【https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaluation_measures_(information_retrieval)】 |
| **Recall@k (R@k)** | **Coverage** of relevant items (did retrieval bring in all needed evidence?). High R@k reduces “missing context” failures. | R@k = (# relevant items in top‑k) / (total # relevant items). | Requires knowing the full set of relevant items. Can be high even if top results are noisy (low precision). | EvidentlyAI defines R@k and gives the formula.【https://www.evidentlyai.com/ranking-metrics/precision-recall-at-k】 Wikipedia gives the general (non‑@k) recall definition.【https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaluation_measures_(information_retrieval)】 |
| **MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank)** | How quickly the **first relevant** chunk appears. Helps when “one good chunk is enough” for the LLM. | For each query: reciprocal rank = 1/(rank of first correct response) or 0 if none; then mean across queries. | Top‑heavy; ignores additional relevant items after the first. | Canonical TREC definition: reciprocal of rank of first correct response (or 0); mean over questions.【https://trec.nist.gov/presentations/TREC8/removed/tsld051.htm】 Also summarized on Wikipedia.【https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_reciprocal_rank】 |
| **MAP (Mean Average Precision)** / **AP** | Overall ranking quality across **multiple** relevant items; rewards ranking relevant evidence early. | AP@k is computed as an average of precision values at ranks where relevant items occur; MAP averages AP over queries. | Good when multiple evidence chunks matter. In this run, a canonical AP formula source was not accessible; the computation description is still usable. | EvidentlyAI: AP@k as average of precision at relevant positions; MAP averages AP across queries.【https://www.evidentlyai.com/ranking-metrics/mean-average-precision-map】 |
| **DCG / nDCG@k** | Ranking quality with **position discounting** and often **graded** relevance (e.g., highly relevant vs somewhat relevant). | DCG sums gains discounted by position; nDCG = DCG / (ideal DCG). | Useful when relevance is graded and rank position strongly matters. | Wikipedia defines DCG and nDCG and states nDCG is DCG normalized by maximum/ideal DCG.【https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discounted_cumulative_gain】 (EvidentlyAI also describes nDCG normalization and provides a DCG formula in text.)【https://www.evidentlyai.com/ranking-metrics/ndcg-metric】 |

**Unresolved (retrieval):** An authoritative, text‑formula source for **HitRate@k / Success@k** was not found in accessible canonical references in this run.

## 2) Context quality metrics (evaluate retrieved context as *input* to generation)

These focus on whether the retrieved context is **useful** and **sufficient** for producing the correct answer.

| Metric | What it measures in RAG | How it’s computed (high level) | Labels needed | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Context Precision (Ragas)** | Whether the retriever ranks **relevant chunks higher than irrelevant** chunks (top-heavy context usefulness). | Ragas states it is “calculated as the mean of the precision@k for each chunk in the context.” | Can be computed “with reference” or “without reference” depending on setup (Ragas describes variants on the metric page). | Ragas stable definition and computation statement.【https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_precision/】 |
| **Context Recall (Ragas)** | Whether retrieval **missed necessary information** (coverage of answer-relevant claims). | Requires a reference: break the reference into claims; check if each claim can be attributed to retrieved context. | **Requires a reference** answer (or reference claims). | Ragas stable definition + “requires a reference” claim-attribution approach.【https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_recall/】 |

## 3) Grounding / faithfulness metrics (evaluate hallucinations vs retrieved evidence)

These ask: **Is the answer supported by the retrieved context?**

| Metric | What it measures in RAG | How it’s computed (high level) | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Faithfulness (Ragas)** | “How factually consistent a response is with the retrieved context”; an answer is faithful if its claims can be supported by context. | Identify claims in the response; check whether each can be inferred from retrieved context; score reflects supported fraction (Ragas example shows computing as a ratio). | Ragas stable definition and calculation steps/example.【https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/faithfulness/】 |
| **Groundedness (TruLens RAG triad)** | Whether response claims have supporting evidence in retrieved context (conceptually the same concern as faithfulness). | TruLens describes splitting response into claims and searching for evidence in the retrieved context for each claim. | TruLens RAG triad groundedness description.【https://www.trulens.org/getting_started/core_concepts/rag_triad/】 |

## 4) Answer quality vs the question (relevance, correctness, factual correctness)

These evaluate the generated answer itself—either **reference-free** (relevance) or **reference-based** (correctness).

| Metric | What it measures in RAG | How it’s computed (high level) | Reference needed? | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Answer/Response Relevancy (Ragas; reference-free)** | How pertinent the generated answer is to the prompt; explicitly **does not consider factuality** (it penalizes incompleteness/redundancy). | Defined as mean cosine similarity between embedding of the original question and embeddings of several “artificial questions” generated from the response. | No | Ragas v0.2.8 page includes definition, caveat (not factuality), and embedding/cosine similarity computation description.【https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.2.8/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/answer_relevance/】 (Similar definition appears in v0.1.21.)【https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.1.21/concepts/metrics/answer_relevance.html】 |
| **Answer Correctness (Ragas)** | Accuracy vs ground truth, combining **semantic similarity** and **factual similarity**. | Combines semantic and factual similarity via a weighted scheme; factual similarity uses TP/FP/FN fact lists and applies an F1 computation over statements. | Yes | Ragas v0.1.21 page defines answer correctness and its semantic+factual composition and TP/FP/FN statement/F1 approach.【https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.1.21/concepts/metrics/answer_correctness.html】 |
| **Factual Correctness (Ragas)** | Factual alignment of response to reference using claim decomposition + NLI to compute overlap (precision/recall/F1 modes). | Break response and reference into claims; use NLI to determine overlap; quantify overlap with precision/recall/F1 (mode controls which). | Yes | Ragas stable definition and overlap scoring modes (incl. “precision mode”).【https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/factual_correctness/】 |
| **(Concept categories) Correctness / Faithfulness / Answer Relevancy (LlamaIndex)** | A common practical decomposition: correctness vs reference, faithfulness to retrieved context, relevance to query. | LlamaIndex describes what each measures (conceptual evaluator types). | Depends on metric | LlamaIndex evaluation guide defines these categories in plain language.【https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/framework/module_guides/evaluating/】 |

### Note on Ragas versions
- The **context precision/recall/faithfulness** pages cited are from **Ragas “stable”** docs (URL contains `/en/stable/`).【https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_precision/】【https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_recall/】【https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/faithfulness/】
- For **answer relevancy** and **answer correctness**, the fully accessible definitions in this run were from **versioned docs** (`v0.2.8`, `v0.1.21`).【https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.2.8/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/answer_relevance/】【https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.1.21/concepts/metrics/answer_correctness.html】 Implementation details may differ across versions; the report reflects the definitions stated on those pages.

## 5) Production/system metrics (evaluate operability, reliability, and cost)

These matter for RAG in production: even “accurate” systems can fail due to latency, errors, or cost.

| Metric | What it measures | How it’s computed (high level) | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P95 latency** | Tail latency: the latency threshold that 95% of requests are at or below (in a window). | Defined as the 95th percentile latency (not an average or max). | SRE School definition of P95 latency and caveats.【https://sreschool.com/blog/p95-latency/】 |
| **Error rate** | Reliability: fraction of requests/operations that fail. | error rate = failed events / total events over a defined window. | SRE School definition + formula.【https://sreschool.com/blog/error-rate/】 |
| **Throughput (tokens/sec, QPS relationship)** | Capacity: how many tokens/queries per unit time the system can handle. | Google Cloud defines: throughput_per_second = (inputs_per_query + outputs_per_query) * queries_per_second; throughput can be measured in tokens/sec. | Google Cloud provisioned throughput measurement definition/equation.【https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/provisioned-throughput/measure-provisioned-throughput】 |
| **Cost per request** | End-to-end unit cost of one logical request through all infra/services (direct + shared). | Cost aggregated per request. | FinOps School definition.【https://finopsschool.com/blog/cost-per-request/】 |
| **Token usage & cost tracking** | Cost drivers at the LLM-call level: units consumed and USD cost per usage type; compute cost by multiplying price by usage. | Track token usage and multiply by configured prices to compute cost. | Langfuse token and cost tracking description (usage + cost details; multiplication).【https://langfuse.com/docs/observability/features/token-and-cost-tracking】 |

## 6) Why overlap-only generation metrics are often insufficient for RAG

Classic n‑gram overlap metrics (e.g., BLEU/ROUGE) are sometimes used when you have references, but they don’t directly measure grounding/faithfulness.

- Elastic notes such n‑gram metrics “fall short” in assessing “meaning,” lack semantic knowledge, and can have “quite low” correlation with human judgments.【https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/evaluating-rag-metrics】

## Conclusions

- RAG evaluation is best done with a **portfolio** of metrics:
  - **Retrieval ranking metrics** (e.g., P@k, R@k, MRR, MAP, nDCG) measure whether relevant evidence is retrieved and how well it is ranked.
  - **Context quality metrics** (Ragas Context Precision/Recall) measure whether the retrieved context is **useful and sufficient** for answering.
  - **Grounding metrics** (Ragas Faithfulness; TruLens groundedness concept) measure whether the answer’s claims are **supported by retrieved evidence**.
  - **Answer-focused metrics** separate **relevance to the question** (Ragas answer relevancy, explicitly not factuality) from **correctness vs reference** (Ragas answer correctness / factual correctness).
  - **System metrics** (p95 latency, error rate, throughput, cost per request, token-cost tracking) are necessary to evaluate real-world RAG performance.

- What stayed unresolved due to source accessibility limits in this run:
  1) a canonical, text-formula definition for **HitRate@k / Success@k**;
  2) canonical text formulas from TREC/textbook sources for **Precision@k, Recall@k, MAP** (the formulas are provided via EvidentlyAI, not a canonical IR textbook);
  3) a widely recognized framework definition for **citation/attribution precision/recall** as a distinct metric (framework pages retrieved focus on groundedness/faithfulness rather than “citation correctness”).
